title: Meta Muse AI Agents Could Reshape the Internet — and Create a New Wave of Online Problems

author.name: Tech Desk
author.bio: The Tech Desk covers the intersection of consumer technology, artificial intelligence, and online security.

excerpt: Meta's Muse AI agent can browse the web, shop, book appointments and manage digital tasks, but experts warn widespread AI agents could create new problems for the internet.
seoTitle: Meta Muse AI Agents Could Reshape the Internet — and Create a New Wave of Online Problems
seoDescription: Meta's Muse AI agent can browse the web, shop, book appointments and manage digital tasks, but experts warn widespread AI agents could create new problems for the internet.

content.text: Meta's new Muse AI agent is designed to do something very different from a conventional chatbot. Rather than simply answering a question, Muse can browse websites, complete tasks, interact with connected applications and continue working in the background on a user's behalf. Meta launched the personal AI agent in September 2026 and has positioned it as a major step toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg calls personal superintelligence. But as the technology moves from generating answers to actually taking actions online, researchers and security specialists are warning that the internet itself may need to change to cope with millions of autonomous software agents.

The concern is not necessarily that Muse itself will deliberately disrupt the web. Instead, the problem could emerge from scale. The internet was largely designed around human users, who browse at relatively slow speeds, make limited numbers of purchases and appointments and usually interact with one website at a time. AI agents can potentially perform many of those activities much faster and with less friction. BBC Future reported that researchers see the possibility of an increasingly crowded online environment in which automated agents compete with humans for limited resources such as concert tickets, restaurant tables and government appointments.

Muse is particularly significant because Meta is making agentic AI accessible to ordinary consumers rather than restricting it to developers or enterprise customers. The company says Muse can handle tasks including booking appointments, filling out forms, managing customer-service interactions, shopping and communicating through connected apps. It runs through a dedicated virtual machine with its own browser, allowing it to operate online on behalf of the user rather than simply providing instructions for the user to follow.

That difference could fundamentally change the way people use websites. Instead of personally visiting a retailer, comparing products and checking out, a user could tell an AI agent what they want and let the software handle the process. Instead of waiting on a customer-service page, an agent could negotiate with a company or submit a cancellation request. These examples are convenient individually, but they create new challenges when thousands or millions of agents attempt similar actions simultaneously.

One of the clearest examples is ticketing and reservations. If an AI agent can automatically search for limited concert tickets, restaurant tables or appointment slots, users may no longer need to compete directly with other humans. They could instead be competing against increasingly sophisticated automated systems. Experts cited by BBC Future warned that this could intensify existing problems surrounding ticket scalping and appointment hoarding, with some people potentially allowing their agents to reserve multiple options because the cost of doing so is minimal.

That could force services to reconsider the familiar “first come, first served” model. Websites may introduce stricter identity verification, lotteries, reservations tied to verified individuals or other measures intended to prevent automated users from overwhelming limited inventory. Such changes would not necessarily eliminate bots, but they could make online transactions more complicated for everyone, including genuine human users. The internet could become more resistant to automation precisely because automation becomes more common.

Small businesses face another potential problem. An AI agent that contacts a company might save a consumer significant time, but thousands of such agents could generate a huge volume of automated inquiries. A small retailer could suddenly receive requests, price negotiations, customer-service messages and scheduling changes from software rather than people. What looks like efficient automation from the customer's perspective could become a new operational burden for the business receiving those requests. BBC Future cited researchers who warned that businesses may struggle if machine-generated interactions become dramatically more frequent than traditional human requests.

The implications extend to the business model of the wider web. Many websites depend on advertising, page views, subscriptions or affiliate clicks. AI agents do not necessarily behave like human visitors. An agent may read information without viewing advertisements, compare several products without spending time on branded pages or complete an entire transaction without generating the sequence of clicks on which publishers and retailers have historically relied. That could weaken parts of the advertising-driven web while increasing the importance of direct machine-to-machine commerce.

Meta is already moving in that direction. On September 29, the company expanded Muse to small businesses and added connections to services including Shopify, QuickBooks, Canva, Slack, Stripe, Notion and other tools. Meta says businesses can use Muse to analyze sales and marketing activity, manage operations, communicate with customers and create content. The expansion shows that Meta is not treating agents merely as personal assistants; it is building a wider software layer through which AI systems can interact with commercial services.

That growth also raises questions about who controls the automated internet. If millions of consumers eventually rely on agents to choose products, book travel or communicate with companies, websites may increasingly optimize their systems for machines rather than people. Businesses could develop special interfaces and pricing structures for AI agents, while platforms may impose access fees or restrict automated traffic. Researchers are already discussing systems in which agents pay websites for machine-readable access rather than scraping information for free.

Security and privacy are equally important. Muse can be connected to highly sensitive services, including email, calendars and other applications. Meta says its system uses a dedicated Secure VM, user permissions, monitoring and other safeguards, and the company says critical actions such as purchases require user approval. Meta has also described specific work on prompt-injection defenses, tool-use safety and monitoring for agent behavior.

Those protections have not eliminated security concerns. Reuters reported on September 25 that Meta strengthened its safety warnings after an external researcher discovered a significant vulnerability involving Muse. According to the report, the flaw potentially allowed attackers to access sensitive personal information stored in Muse's virtual machines, including emails and files. Reuters also reported that Muse had accumulated about 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks, highlighting how quickly a vulnerability in a widely adopted agent could become consequential.

There have been other demonstrations of the unusual security surface created by agentic systems. The Verge reported that researchers were able to prompt Muse into revealing parts of its filesystem, including system files, templates and internal documentation. Meta said Muse operates inside isolated virtual machines and that the behavior did not expose Meta's infrastructure or other users' data. Even so, the incident illustrates how an AI agent's ability to interact with a computer introduces security questions that are different from those associated with traditional chatbots.

The potential risks are therefore broader than spam or annoying website behavior. An agent may make decisions on a user's behalf, and the user may not always know exactly why a particular choice was made. If Muse recommends a hotel, product or service, for example, users may have to trust that the recommendation genuinely reflects their interests rather than hidden commercial incentives. Meta says Muse is designed around user control and that its safeguards are intended to keep people in charge, but researchers continue to argue that agentic systems require stronger rules governing how automated decisions interact with commercial services.

The scale of adoption could make these questions urgent. Reuters reported that Muse had become one of the fastest-growing new AI products after its September 8 launch, while other companies are releasing competing agents of their own. OpenAI has also entered the market with its new Dots agents, indicating that personal AI systems are becoming a major competitive category rather than a single-company experiment.

Meta itself is preparing for an even more connected version of Muse. At Connect 2026, the company announced plans to bring Muse to its AI glasses, expand the number of connectors available to the agent and give Muse its own email address. The company also unveiled Muse Charm, a small dedicated device for interacting with the assistant through voice. Those developments suggest that Meta wants Muse to move beyond an app and become a persistent digital layer available throughout a user's day.

That could produce genuine benefits. AI agents may reduce repetitive administrative work, help people navigate complicated digital systems and give small businesses access to capabilities that previously required specialists. They could also make online services more accessible to people who find complex websites difficult to use. The challenge is that the architecture of the internet was created before software agents were capable of acting independently at this scale.

Researchers quoted by BBC Future argue that the answer will eventually involve new “rules of the road” for AI agents. Websites could distinguish between humans and automated agents, establish standardized machine-access protocols, charge for automated usage or require agents to follow explicit limits. Regulators may also face questions about accountability when an automated system causes financial loss, overwhelms a service or makes a consequential decision.

For now, the transition is happening faster than the rules surrounding it. Meta has released Muse, competitors are following, and consumers are beginning to delegate more of their online lives to software. The promise is an internet where tedious tasks disappear and digital services become easier to navigate. The risk is an internet filled with millions of automated actors all pursuing their users' interests at machine speed.

Muse therefore may be remembered not simply as another AI assistant, but as part of the moment when AI agents began interacting with the web at mainstream scale. Whether that makes the internet faster and more useful or more crowded, restrictive and unpredictable will depend on how businesses, platforms, regulators and AI companies redesign online systems around the presence of machines as active participants. The technology is already here; the infrastructure and rules to manage its consequences are still catching up.
